questions_and_answers.question_text: Where does the modifying clause come in Chinese?
Where does the word "reason" come in English?
Which word should be used for "reason"/"cause"?
Write the Chinese for "the reason I came late."
Give the three English glosses of mùdì.
Write the Chinese for "The reason I called you is that I would like to talk with you in person."

answers.answer_text: Wǒ gěi ni dǎ diànhuàde mùdì shi xiǎng gēn ni dāngmiàn tántan.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Which marker links the modifying clause to mùdì?
Is mùdì the right word for "cause"?

answers.answer_text: No — yuányīn should be used for "reason" or "cause."

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "All right. When?"

articles.text:
5. A: Wǒ gěi ni dǎ diànhuàde mùdì    The reason I called you is that I
      shi xiǎng gēn ni dāngmiàn       would like to talk with you in
      tántan.                         person.
   B: Hǎo a. Shénme shíhou a?        All right. When?

Note on No. 5

Wǒ gěi ni dǎ diànhuàde mùdì shi...: In English, the word "reason," or "purpose," begins the phrase, with the modifying clause following. In Chinese, everything modifying "the purpose" precedes mùdì.

Wǒ gěi ni dǎ diànhuà | -de | mùdì | shi... .
(The reason why I called you is... .)

Mùdì, "purpose," "aim," "objective": Although translated idiomatically as "reason" in exchange 5, mùdì does not really mean "reason"/"cause." The English terms should be translated as yuányīn: wǒ láiwǎnde yuányīn, "the reason I came late."
